phonemes.desc: Voiceless dental fricative [θ], the thorn; it is the hard 'th' of 'thin', not the voiced 'th' of 'this'
Long open-mid back [ɔː] with acute marking stress and length
Long or geminated alveolar trill [rː], written double in Old Norse to show length

pronunciation.approximation: 'THORR' — begin with the breathy 'th' of 'thin', hold the 'o' long like 'awe', and trill the final r slightly longer than usual.

kin.form: Donar, the continental Germanic thunder god

kin.label: Proto-Germanic

pronunciation.note: Þórr is Tier 1: the acute on ó marks stress and length on the first syllable, and the thorn Þ is a distinctive letter — features the ASCII form loses — while the geminate rr preserves the Old Norse long consonant. The English name Thor has lost both the thorn sound and the long rolled r.

domains.title: Thunder, Storms, Oak
domains.subtitle: The domain of Þórr
domains.lead: Þórr is the thunder and the protection it promises: guardian of Ásgarðr and of every farmstead beneath it, wielder of Mjölnir, the hammer that levels giants and hallows weddings alike. Where Óðinn traffics in runes and deceit, Þórr answers with straight force — the god of farmers, sailors and householders, whose oath is the storm's.

cards.name: Mjölnir
cards.desc: The short-handled hammer forged by the dwarfs Brokkr and Sindri — it never misses, always returns, and consecrates brides, births and pyres as readily as it shatters giants (Snorri, Skáldskaparmál 35).

cards.name: Þrymskviða
cards.desc: Disguised as Freyja in bridal linen, Þórr let the giant Þrymr lay Mjölnir in his lap to hallow the bride — then killed every jötunn in the hall (Poetic Edda, Þrymskviða).

cards.name: Hymiskviða
cards.desc: With an ox-head for bait he hooked Jörmungandr, the world-serpent, and dragged it boiling to the surface — Hymir cut the line in terror (Hymiskviða; Gylfaginning 48).

cards.name: Oak and Storm
cards.desc: His oak stands where lightning strikes; sailors blessed their ships and farmers their fields in his name, and his day — Þórsdagr — is Thursday.

symbols.name: Mjöllnir
symbols.meaning: The short-handled hammer that returns to his hand and strikes down giants

symbols.name: Járngreipr (iron gloves)
symbols.meaning: The gloves that allow Thor to grasp the hammer's searing haft

symbols.name: Megingjörð (strength belt)
symbols.meaning: The belt that doubles Thor's already formidable strength

symbols.name: Goat-drawn chariot
symbols.meaning: Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjóstr, the goats who pull his thundering cart

symbols.name: Oak tree
symbols.meaning: The tree sacred to Thor in Germanic folk practice, struck by lightning

mythology.lead: Þórr is the Æsir's enforcer: Mjölnir in hand, he keeps the giants beyond the fence of the world and rides out in a cart drawn by the goats Tanngnjóstr and Tanngrisnir, whose rumble is thunder. The Eddas cast him as the defender of order — sometimes comic, never trivial.

myths.title: The Recovery of Mjölnir
myths.text: When Þórr woke to find Mjölnir gone, his first thought was for the giants: with the hammer lost, their old terror was lost too. The thief proved to be Þrymr, who would return it only for Freyja as bride. The goddess, enraged, refused; Heimdallr proposed the stratagem. They dressed Þórr in bridal linen and keys, hung the necklace Brísingamen on him, veiled his beard, and sent him east with Loki as his handmaid. At the wedding Þrymr grew suspicious at the bride's appetite — a whole ox, eight salmon, three casks of mead — but Loki explained that Freyja had fasted eight nights in longing. Then Þrymr ordered the hammer laid in the bride's lap to hallow her, and the moment Mjölnir touched his knee Þórr laughed aloud: he killed Þrymr and every giant in the hall (Poetic Edda, Þrymskviða). The poem is the Eddas' greatest comedy, but its premise is dead serious: without Mjölnir the gods cannot defend the world. And its comedy has a moral — Þórr's strength is so secure it can survive a wedding dress; order endures because power is willing to play the fool.

myths.title: Fishing for the Miðgarðsormr
myths.text: At Ægir's feast the gods needed a cauldron big enough to brew for them all, and only the giant Hymir owned one a mile deep. Þórr went with Týr to fetch it, slew Hymir's herd of oxen for dinner — the giant raged — and at dawn bullied him into a fishing trip, demanding the giant's best bait: the head of the fine ox Himinhrjóðr. Far out, Þórr rowed beyond the giant's comfort, hooked Jörmungandr, the world-serpent, and hauled the venom-dripping, world-encircling monster up over the gunwale; Hymir, grey with fear, cut the line. In Snorri's version the serpent glares up and Þórr strikes its head with Mjölnir as it sinks, and Hymir remarks that they will not fish together again (Hymiskviða; Gylfaginning 48). The myth makes Þórr the one god who tests the world's seams: he alone dares to drag the creature that holds Miðgarðr together out of its own sea — and every time it slips back, Ragnarǫk comes one fight closer.

myths.title: The Journey to Geirröðr
myths.text: Trapped by the giant Geirröðr, Loki ransomed himself by swearing to bring Þórr to the giant's hall unarmed. Þórr set out without Mjölnir, without Megingjörð, without Járngreipr — stripped of everything that made him Þórr. The giantess Gríðr, mother of Víðarr, found him on the road and lent him her own belt of strength, her iron gloves, and her staff Gríðarvǫlr, warning him of the trap: a chair of lava, two rivers, a glowing iron in the forge. Þórr waded the rising Vimur, jammed the staff in the riverbed, and swept on. In the hall Geirröðr hurled the glowing missile at him; Þórr caught it in the borrowed glove and threw it back through the giant, through the pillar behind him, through the wall and into the ground — so that every jötunn in the hall died where he stood (Snorri, Skáldskaparmál 17; the skald Eilífr Goðrúnarson's Þórsdrápa). The tale teaches that Þórr's true weapon is not the hammer but the return of violence to its sender: whatever is thrown at him comes back.

myths.title: The One God Loki Could Not Talk Around
myths.text: At Ægir's banquet Loki, uninvited, went from god to god with insults honed to wound — accusing Óðinn of oath-breaking, Týr of cuckoldry, Frigg and Freyja of unchastity. The gods endured him in silence: a guest beneath the roof could not be struck. Then Þórr came in from the east, from his journey, and the talk changed. 'Hold your tongue, Loki,' he said, 'or Mjölnir will shut it.' Loki mocked him too — but only once, and from the doorway: he had spoken before all the Æsir, he says, yet 'for you alone will I go out, since you threaten with the hammer.' He left, was seized in the Franangr falls, and bound in the guts of his own son (Poetic Edda, Lokasenna). The poem's architecture is its meaning: every god can be talked around, bought or shamed — except the thunderer. Words lose to the hammer; order keeps its enforcer, and Loki's first moment of prudence is his first acknowledgment of Þórr's.

myths.title: Nine Steps
myths.text: The seeress of the Völuspá foretold the end: the hound Garmr bays before Gnipahellir, the sky splits, and Jörmungandr rises from the poisoned sea to spill venom over sky and earth. Þórr meets his old fishing-quarry one last time and destroys it — but as the serpent dies it pours venom over him, and Þórr walks nine steps and falls (Völuspá 55–56; Snorri, Gylfaginning 51). The strongest of the gods is killed by the very thing he conquered. Yet the Völuspá does not end there: the earth rises green again from the sea, Baldr returns, and Þórr's sons Móði and Magni inherit Mjölnir 'when the gods return' — and Magni boasts his father would be praised. The myth gives Germanic heroism its formula: not survival, but having saved the world first — strength in the service of order, spent to the last drop, and the hammer passed on.

lore.syncretism: Rome read Þórr as her own thunderer, and the weekday names say it: Latin dies Jovis became Old English Þunresdæg, German Donnerstag and English Thursday, mapping the Norse god onto Jupiter by function. Medieval writers drew the same parallel differently: Adam of Bremen describes the great temple at Uppsala where 'Thor, the mightiest', sits enthroned between Wodan and Fricco, master of thunder and lightning, and Saxo Grammaticus rationalizes him as a usurping warrior whose hammer-strokes were long remembered. The Hercules comparison recurred as well, since both bludgeon chaos-monsters. Under Christianization the cult left durable fossils: Mjölnir amulets are found in graves beside crosses, and his name survives in hundreds of Scandinavian place-names and in the English weekday. The nineteenth-century romantic revival — and after it, modern Ásatrú — restored him from folklore to godhood, a journey no other Germanic deity travelled quite so far.
lore.culturalLegacy: Þórr never left daily life: his weekday, Thursday, is spoken weekly by hundreds of millions who never think of him. Hundreds of Scandinavian place-names — Torslanda, Thorsager and their kin — pin his cult to the map, and runestones from the Glavendrup stone ('may Thor hallow these runes') to the Altuna stone's serpent-fishing scene kept his image in stone. In the twentieth century he leapt to comics and film, where the Marvel Thor both popularizes and flattens him; meanwhile modern Ásatrú and heathen communities have re-sacralized Mjölnir as a pendant — a symbol now also contested by movements seeking borrowed Norse prestige. The medieval god of farmers and sailors endures because he was always the people's god: his cult was never an aristocracy's property, and so it could not be buried with one.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Þórr is strength that knows its job. He is the strongest of the gods and almost never the cleverest, and the Eddas treat that as a virtue: the world does not need its thunder to scheme. While Óðinn buys wisdom with an eye and a hanging, Þórr travels, fishes, dresses as a bride, loses his temper — and keeps the giants on their side of the fence. His hammer consecrates weddings, births, funerals and fields; Germanic oath-language invoked him, as the Glavendrup stone still testifies. He is, in short, the god of the unglamorous majority — farmers, sailors, householders — whose protection was expected daily, not mystically.

Restoring his name in Old Norse dress — thorn Þ, acute ó, geminate rr — matters precisely because that majority is where the name lived. Þórr is not the thunder of the cosmos; he is the thunder that walks home.

lore.archaeology: The Altuna runestone in Uppland (U 1161) depicts Þórr fishing for the Miðgarðsormr, the most direct pictorial attestation of his myth. Mjölnir pendants are found by the thousand from Birka, Hedeby, and across the Norse diaspora; the Eyrarland bronze statuette from Iceland may represent the thunder-god with his hammer. The Jelling stones and runestones such as the Glavendrup stone invoke his protection.
